unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramble & Rowan Outfitters is a private limited company running 5 clothing stores in Country X. It employs 32 sales assistants selling men's and women's casual clothing at mid-range prices. Last year the business reported revenue of $2,400,000 and a gross profit margin of 42%, and it competes mainly on price and store location.

The Country X government has announced that the basic rate of income tax will rise from 20% to 25% from April, reducing the disposable income of many of the store's customers. Footfall across the 5 stores has already fallen by 8% this year. Management is debating whether to cut prices to stimulate demand or to hold prices steady and accept lower sales volumes in the coming trading year.

questions.question_text: Define 'income tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax that individuals pay on the income they earn, such as wages and salaries. The amount paid usually rises as income increases [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax paid by individuals on income/wages/salaries
amount rises as income increases / deducted by the government

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the rise in income tax on Bramble & Rowan Outfitters.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Lower disposable income for customers [k], so shoppers at the 5 stores keep less of their pay after tax and buy fewer mid-range casual clothes [app]. Effect 2: Falling sales revenue [k], adding to the 8% drop in footfall already seen this year across the company's stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: customers have less disposable income / reduced spending power
sales revenue falls / demand declines

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the rise in income tax could affect Bramble & Rowan's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Customers have reduced disposable income [k], so after the basic rate of income tax rises to 25% they keep less of their wages [app], which means non-essential purchases like casual clothing are cut first [an]. Way 2: Customers become more price-sensitive [k], so shoppers compare Bramble & Rowan's mid-range prices against discounters [app], leading some to switch to cheaper stores and reducing the company's sales volumes [an].

knowledge_max_2: reduced disposable income
greater price sensitivity / switching to cheaper substitutes
application_max_2: basic rate of income tax rises from 20% to 25%
analysis_max_2: non-essential purchases are cut first
customers switch to discount retailers, reducing sales volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramble & Rowan Outfitters should cut its prices rather than hold prices steady? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting prices could stimulate demand [k] by attracting price-sensitive shoppers back to the 5 stores after footfall already fell by 8% [app], lifting sales volumes and using the 42% gross profit margin to cushion lower prices [an]. Holding prices steady protects the margin [k] and preserves profit per item on $2,400,000 of last year's revenue [app], avoiding a price war with competitors that could further erode profitability [an]. On one hand, holding prices steady risks further footfall declines [eval]; on the other hand, cutting prices may fail to offset lower margins if disposable incomes keep falling after the tax rise to 25% [eval]. Overall, cutting prices moderately is the stronger option because footfall has already dropped 8% and the business needs traffic through its stores to protect total profit, even though margins will narrow.

knowledge_max_2: price cut stimulates demand / attracts shoppers
holding prices protects margin / profit per item
analysis_max_2: lower prices lift volume using the margin cushion
holding prices risks further traffic decline and no volume recovery
evaluation_max_2: weighs price cut against price hold in light of the tax rise
justified recommendation referencing footfall and margin

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ironquay Engineering Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing industrial water pumps for farms and factories in Country X. It employs 84 production staff and reported revenue of $3,600,000 last year, making a profit of $540,000 before tax is deducted. The company's workshop operates 2 shifts on most weekdays.

The Country X government has announced that corporation tax on company profits will rise from 19% to 25% next year. At current profit levels this adds $32,400 a year to the company's tax bill. Management must decide whether to reduce the dividend paid to its family shareholders or to postpone a planned $500,000 expansion of its factory and warehouse, which would be financed by a bank loan repaid over 6 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'corporation tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax charged on the profits earned by companies and paid to the government. The amount paid depends on the level of profit made [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax charged on company profits
paid to the government / depends on profit level

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the rise in corporation tax on Ironquay Engineering Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: A higher tax bill [k], with the rise from 19% to 25% adding $32,400 a year to the amount the company pays [app]. Effect 2: Lower retained profit [k], leaving less internal finance available from the $540,000 pre-tax profit to fund the planned factory expansion [app].

knowledge_max_2: higher tax bill / more tax paid
less retained profit / less internal finance
application_max_2: rise from 19% to 25% adding $32,400 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the business may face if it reduces the dividend paid to shareholders.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Shareholders may be dissatisfied [k], because family shareholders of the private limited company expect a return on their investment [app], which could lead to conflict or a loss of confidence in management [an]. Problem 2: Dividends are the main reward for shareholders [k], so cutting the dividend reduces their income after tax [app], making the shares less attractive to any future outside investors [an].

knowledge_max_2: shareholders expect a return / dividends are a reward
shareholders may be dissatisfied / conflict with owners
application_max_2: family shareholders of the private limited company
reduce the dividend to fund the expansion
analysis_max_2: loss of confidence in management / owner conflict
shares become less attractive to outside investors

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironquay Engineering should reduce the dividend rather than postpone the factory expansion? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Reducing the dividend keeps the expansion on track [k] because it preserves cash for the planned $500,000 factory and warehouse expansion [app], which should lower unit costs and raise competitiveness for the company's industrial water pumps [an]. However, family shareholders rely on dividend income [k] and may resist a cut to their returns from the $3,600,000 revenue business [app], straining relationships in a close family-owned company [an]. On one hand, postponing the expansion avoids shareholder conflict [eval]; on the other hand, delaying it forfeits long-term savings while the tax bill rises by $32,400 a year [eval]. Overall, reducing the dividend is the stronger option because the expansion, repaid over 6 years, should generate returns that outweigh the short-term dividend loss.

knowledge_max_2: reducing dividend preserves cash for investment
shareholders rely on dividend income
analysis_max_2: expansion lowers unit costs / raises competitiveness
cutting dividend strains family shareholder relationships
evaluation_max_2: weighs shareholder income loss against expansion gains
justified recommendation referencing the expansion payback over 6 years

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kettle & Rye Café is a private limited company operating 3 cafés in Country X. It employs 26 staff and serves around 3,200 customers a week, selling breakfasts, lunches and coffee to commuters and nearby office workers. Last year the business had sales of $1,500,000, with an average meal costing $9 and an average gross profit margin of 55% before any tax changes.

The Country X government will raise value added tax (VAT), an indirect tax on goods and services, from 10% to 14% next quarter. Management is deciding whether to absorb the extra tax, cutting its profit margin, or to increase menu prices by 4% across the board. The two nearest competing cafés have not yet announced any price rises for their customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'value added tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax charged on goods and services at the point of sale, collected by the business and passed on to the government [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax on goods and services / indirect tax
collected by business and passed to government

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the VAT rise on Kettle & Rye Café.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: A higher tax on each sale [k], with VAT rising from 10% to 14% on every meal sold to the 3,200 customers served each week [app]. Effect 2: A choice between absorbing or passing on the tax [k], because absorbing it cuts the 55% gross profit margin while raising prices risks losing trade to the two competing cafés [app].

knowledge_max_2: higher tax per sale / VAT collected increases
must absorb the tax or raise prices
application_max_2: 3,200 customers a week / 55% gross profit margin

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the VAT rise could affect the café's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Higher menu prices [k], so if the café adds 4% to prices customers pay more for their average $9 meal [app], reducing real spending power and possibly how often they eat out [an]. Way 2: Switching to competitors [k], as customers may choose the two nearest competing cafés that have not raised prices [app], leaving the café with fewer customers and lower sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher prices / real spending power falls
customers switch to cheaper alternatives
application_max_2: menu prices increased by 4% / average $9 meal
two nearest competing cafés have not raised prices
analysis_max_2: customers cut spending on eating out
café loses customers to rivals, reducing sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Kettle & Rye Café should absorb the VAT rise rather than increase menu prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Absorbing the rise protects customer loyalty [k] because prices stay the same for the 3,200 customers served weekly [app], helping the café avoid losing trade to the two competing cafés that have not raised prices [an]. However, absorbing the tax cuts the 55% gross profit margin [k] and squeezes profit on every meal sold at an average of $9 [app], which could weaken cash flow for the business [an]. On one hand, holding prices steady may win market share while rivals raise prices [eval]; on the other hand, the 4% menu price increase would restore margins if demand stays buoyant [eval]. Overall, absorbing the VAT rise in the short term is the better option, because the café risks losing commuters to rivals and must defend $1,500,000 of annual sales.

knowledge_max_2: absorbing tax protects customer loyalty / prices stable
absorbing tax squeezes profit margin
analysis_max_2: avoids losing trade to competing cafés
weakens cash flow if margins fall
evaluation_max_2: weighs price-hold market share gain against margin loss
justified recommendation referencing competitor behaviour

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Greyfen Textiles Ltd is a private limited company weaving polyester fabric for garment makers in Country X. It employs 64 weavers on 3 production lines and reported revenue of $2,900,000 last year, supplying fabric to 22 clothing factories across the country and abroad.

The Country X government has introduced a 15% import tariff on fabric imports from abroad. Greyfen imports 70% of its raw fabric and its annual imported fabric bill is $800,000, so the tariff will add $120,000 a year to its production costs. A domestic fabric supplier charges 20% more than the imported price but can deliver within 2 weeks of ordering. Management must decide whether to switch to the domestic supplier or to absorb the tariff cost and keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'import tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed on goods imported from other countries, paid by the importing business when the goods cross the border [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax on imports / imported goods
paid by the importer at the border

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the import tariff on Greyfen Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Higher production costs [k], as the 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year on top of the $800,000 imported fabric bill [app]. Effect 2: Lower profit margin or higher prices [k], because Greyfen must either absorb the extra $120,000 cost from revenue of $2,900,000 or raise prices for its 22 clothing factory customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: higher costs / higher import bill
lower profit margin or higher prices
application_max_2: 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year to the $800,000 fabric bill

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a government might impose import tariffs.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To protect domestic producers [k], for example a Country X fabric supplier would benefit if Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources [app], helping domestic firms compete and keeping jobs in the country [an]. Reason 2: To raise government revenue [k], collecting the 15% tariff on Greyfen's $800,000 fabric imports would yield $120,000 a year [app], which the government can spend on public services [an].

knowledge_max_2: protect domestic industry / domestic jobs
raise government revenue / public spending
application_max_2: Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources
analysis_max_2: domestic firms become more competitive
tariff revenue funds public services

questions.question_text: Do you think Greyfen Textiles should switch to the domestic fabric supplier rather than absorb the tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to the domestic supplier avoids the $120,000 tariff [k], because domestic fabric priced 20% above imports removes the border tax on $800,000 of fabric [app], and deliveries within 2 weeks improve reliability for its 22 clothing factory customers [an]. However, the domestic price is 20% higher than imports [k], adding around $160,000 a year to the fabric bill [app], which exceeds the $120,000 cost of the tariff [an]. On one hand, absorbing the tariff keeps annual costs $40,000 lower [eval]; on the other hand, domestic sourcing supports Country X jobs and removes import risk [eval]. Overall, absorbing the tariff is the stronger short-term option, because $120,000 a year is cheaper than the domestic premium, but Greyfen should renegotiate with the domestic supplier and review its sourcing next year.

knowledge_max_2: switching avoids the tariff / domestic delivery is faster
domestic price is 20% higher / tariff is cheaper
analysis_max_2: absorbing keeps costs lower by $40,000 a year
domestic sourcing removes import risk and supports local jobs
evaluation_max_2: weighs tariff cost against domestic premium
justified recommendation with review next year

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppergate Civil Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that builds roads, bridges and drainage schemes for public and private clients across 4 regions of the country. It employs 120 engineers and site workers and reported revenue of $9,000,000 last year with a healthy order book for work.

The Country X government has announced a $250 million infrastructure programme to upgrade the national road network over 5 years. Coppergate could bid for a 2-year government contract worth $3,500,000, but it would need to invest $800,000 in new heavy equipment, financed by a bank loan from its usual lender. Management is debating whether to bid for the contract or to keep serving its existing private clients in the region.

questions.question_text: Define 'government spending'.
questions.model_answer: Money spent by the government on public services, infrastructure and transfer payments such as benefits and subsidies [2].

knowledge_max_2: government expenditure on public goods/services
includes infrastructure, benefits and subsidies

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Coppergate of the government's infrastructure programme.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: New contract opportunities [k], because the $250 million road upgrade programme includes tenders such as a 2-year contract worth $3,500,000 that Coppergate could bid for [app]. Benefit 2: Increased demand for its services [k], as government infrastructure spending raises orders for civil engineering firms like Coppergate, which already reported $9,000,000 of revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: new contract opportunities / tenders available
increased demand for civil engineering services

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the business may face if it borrows $800,000 to finance the equipment for the government contract.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Interest payments increase costs [k], so repayments on the $800,000 bank loan reduce the profit earned from the $3,500,000 contract [app], squeezing cash flow in the early months of the project [an]. Problem 2: Risk if the bid fails [k], because winning is not guaranteed and Coppergate could be left with new heavy equipment and loan repayments without the government contract revenue [app], raising financial pressure on the business [an].

knowledge_max_2: interest payments raise costs / cash flow squeezed
winning the bid is not guaranteed / risk of stranded investment
application_max_2: new heavy equipment with no contract revenue if the bid fails
analysis_max_2: repayments reduce profit early in the project
stranded equipment raises financial pressure

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppergate should bid for the government infrastructure contract rather than continue serving private clients? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Bidding would secure a 2-year contract worth $3,500,000 [k], giving Coppergate a large, stable government-backed order to anchor its $9,000,000 revenue business [app], improving capacity utilisation and future credibility for winning public work [an]. However, the bid requires $800,000 of new heavy equipment financed by a bank loan [k], adding repayments that strain cash flow before the contract pays out [app], and execution risk is high if costs overrun or the bid is lost [an]. On one hand, private clients offer faster payment and flexible work [eval]; on the other hand, the government contract's guaranteed scale and prestige could transform the company [eval]. Overall, Coppergate should bid, because the $3,500,000 contract and the $250 million programme signal sustained public spending that will outlast individual private jobs.

knowledge_max_2: bidding secures guaranteed work / anchors revenue
bid requires heavy investment and loan repayments
analysis_max_2: improves capacity utilisation and public-sector credibility
repayments strain cash flow before revenue arrives
evaluation_max_2: weighs stable public work against flexible private work
justified recommendation referencing the programme's scale

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Sunhollow Dairy Farm is a sole trader farm run by Marta Ellison in Country X. It employs 14 farm workers and produces organic milk, generating revenue of $620,000 last year from 220 dairy cows grazing on rented pasture near the coast.

The Country X government provides an annual subsidy of $90,000 to support organic milk production and animal welfare standards on the farm. From next year the subsidy will be cut by half to $45,000, as government spending will shift towards renewable energy projects elsewhere. The owner must decide whether to continue organic production with lower support or to switch to conventional dairy farming instead, which could earn $700,000 a year but requires $150,000 of new milking equipment and fewer staff.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A payment made by the government to producers or firms to reduce their costs or to encourage production of a particular good or service [2].

knowledge_max_2: payment by government to producers
reduces costs / encourages production

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the subsidy cut on Sunhollow Dairy Farm.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Reduced income [k], as the subsidy falls by half from $90,000 to $45,000, removing $45,000 of support each year [app]. Effect 2: Lower profitability or pressure to change production [k], because the farm's $620,000 revenue must now cover more of its costs itself [app].

knowledge_max_2: reduced income / less government support
lower profitability / pressure to change production

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a government provides subsidies to farmers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To keep food affordable [k], because supporting organic milk production like Sunhollow's helps maintain supply and restrains price rises for consumers [app], stabilising the cost of living [an]. Reason 2: To protect rural employment and the environment [k], since the $90,000 subsidy supports 14 farm workers on Sunhollow and encourages organic, welfare-friendly methods [app], preserving local jobs and sustainable farming [an].

knowledge_max_2: keep food affordable / secure food supply
protect rural employment / encourage sustainable farming
analysis_max_2: stabilises the cost of living
preserves local jobs and sustainable methods

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunhollow Dairy Farm should continue organic production rather than switch to conventional dairy farming? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Continuing organic production preserves the farm's identity [k], keeping the organic milk that generated $620,000 of revenue and maintaining animal welfare standards [app], and retaining loyal customers who pay a premium for organic produce [an]. However, switching to conventional farming could earn $700,000 a year [k], $80,000 more than current organic revenue [app], but it requires $150,000 of new milking equipment and loses the remaining $45,000 subsidy [an]. On one hand, the subsidy cut makes organic production marginal [eval]; on the other hand, switching costs and losing organic buyers create their own risks [eval]. Overall, Sunhollow should continue organic production for now, because the revenue difference is modest relative to $150,000 of new equipment, but it should review the decision if subsidies fall further.

knowledge_max_2: organic preserves identity / loyal premium customers
switching earns more but needs investment
application_max_2: organic milk generated $620,000 / switching could earn $700,000
analysis_max_2: loyal customers pay a premium, protecting demand
switching forfeits subsidy and organic buyers
evaluation_max_2: weighs organic margin loss against switching gains
justified recommendation with conditional review

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Pennybrook Discount Stores is a private limited company operating 9 discount supermarkets in Country X. It employs 85 staff and reported revenue of $7,200,000 last year, with an average basket value of $18 per customer visit. Most of its customers have low incomes and live within walking distance of the stores.

The Country X government has announced cuts of 12% to means-tested welfare payments from January, reducing the disposable income of many households on low incomes. The director believes shoppers will trade down from full-price supermarkets to discounters like Pennybrook over the next year. The board is debating whether to open a tenth store in a nearby town or to improve the layout and capacity of its existing nine stores locally.

questions.question_text: Define 'disposable income'.
questions.model_answer: The income individuals have left to spend or save after income tax and other deductions have been paid [2].

knowledge_max_2: income left after tax/deductions
available to spend or save

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the welfare payment cuts on Pennybrook's customers.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Lower disposable income [k], because the 12% cut to means-tested welfare payments leaves low-income households with less money to spend each week [app]. Effect 2: Reduced spending on non-essentials [k], so customers using the $18 average basket focus on essentials and cheaper own-label goods [app].

knowledge_max_2: lower disposable income
reduced spending on non-essentials / essentials prioritised

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the benefits cut could affect Pennybrook Discount Stores.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Increased demand for discount groceries [k], as cash-strapped shoppers trade down from full-price supermarkets to Pennybrook's stores [app], potentially increasing footfall and sales revenue [an]. Way 2: Smaller average basket size [k], because customers with less disposable income may buy fewer items per visit even at discount prices [app], so revenue gains depend on attracting many more customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: demand for discount groceries rises
average basket size may shrink
application_max_2: shoppers trade down from full-price supermarkets
analysis_max_2: footfall and sales revenue may rise
revenue gains depend on attracting more customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Pennybrook should open a tenth store rather than improve its existing nine stores? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening a tenth store captures the expected wave of trade-down shoppers [k], expanding Pennybrook's reach beyond its current 9 stores and 85 staff [app], and building long-term revenue if the welfare cuts persist [an]. However, a new store requires heavy capital spending [k], and sales per store may fall if the trade-down boom is modest or short-lived [app], while the existing nine stores already serve local low-income communities well [an]. On one hand, improving the nine existing stores costs less and lifts capacity where demand is proven [eval]; on the other hand, a tenth store locks in market share before rivals respond [eval]. Overall, improving the existing nine stores first is the safer option, because demand uplift from the welfare cuts is uncertain, and Pennybrook can invest later once the trading-down trend is clearly visible in the $7,200,000 revenue figures.

knowledge_max_2: opening a new store captures trade-down demand
new store requires heavy capital spending
analysis_max_2: locks in long-term revenue if welfare cuts persist
improving existing stores costs less with proven demand
evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion risk against low-cost capacity upgrade
justified recommendation to improve existing stores first

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bluebell Schoolwear Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing school uniforms in Country X. It employs 45 machinists at a single factory and reported revenue of $1,800,000 last year, supplying shirts, trousers and blazers to retailers and schools across the whole country.

The Country X government is inviting tenders for a 3-year contract to supply uniforms to 40 state schools, guaranteeing $600,000 of orders a year at a profit margin of only 8%. Private retail clients currently give the business a margin of 20%, but their order volumes are uncertain from season to season and very hard to predict in advance. Management must decide whether to bid for the government contract or to focus on its private retail customers instead.

questions.question_text: Define 'revenue'.
questions.model_answer: The total income a business receives from selling its goods or services before any costs are deducted [2].

knowledge_max_2: total income from sales of goods/services
measured before costs are deducted

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the government contract for Bluebell Schoolwear.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Guaranteed orders [k], with the 3-year contract assuring $600,000 of uniform orders a year from 40 state schools [app]. Benefit 2: Steady production planning [k], because guaranteed government orders make output and staffing for the 45 machinists easier to schedule than uncertain retail demand [app].

knowledge_max_2: guaranteed orders / secure revenue stream
easier production and staff scheduling
application_max_2: 3-year contract assuring $600,000 of orders a year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for the business of bidding for the government contract.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A very low profit margin [k], because the contract offers only an 8% margin compared with 20% from private retail clients [app], so extra revenue adds little profit to the bottom line [an]. Problem 2: Tendering costs and uncertainty [k], because preparing bids for 40 state schools consumes management time [app], and the business may win at a price that barely covers production costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: very low profit margin on the contract
tendering consumes time / risk of winning at too low a price
analysis_max_2: extra revenue adds little profit
management time diverted from retail clients

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluebell Schoolwear should bid for the government contract rather than focus on private retail customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Bidding secures guaranteed volume [k], anchoring $600,000 of annual orders over 3 years from 40 state schools [app], which improves capacity utilisation and cash flow predictability for the factory [an]. However, the 8% margin is far below the 20% earned from private clients [k], squeezing profit on $1,800,000 of revenue [app], and management time spent tendering could distract from higher-margin retail work [an]. On one hand, private clients offer better profitability but volatile demand [eval]; on the other hand, the government contract offers stability at thin margins [eval]. Overall, Bluebell should bid, because guaranteed $600,000 annual revenue and full utilisation of its 45 machinists reduce risk, and the retail business can continue alongside the contract.

knowledge_max_2: bidding secures guaranteed volume / stability
8% margin is far below the 20% retail margin
analysis_max_2: improves utilisation and cash flow predictability
tendering distracts from higher-margin retail
evaluation_max_2: weighs retail profitability against contract stability
justified recommendation to bid with retail continuing

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Halcyon Motors is a car dealership in Country X selling new and used family cars. It employs 18 sales staff and reported revenue of $3,200,000 last year, selling 160 cars at an average price of $20,000, mainly to local families in the town.

The Country X government has announced an increase in the income tax personal allowance from $12,000 to $13,500, so many households will keep an extra $1,500 of income a year. The director expects demand for new cars to rise over the next 12 months as consumer confidence slowly improves. Management must decide whether to order more new-car stock from manufacturers or to expand its part-exchange and used-car operation, which has lower profit per unit but lower risk.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax charged directly on income or wealth, paid straight to the government by the individual or organisation, such as income tax [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax on income or wealth
paid directly to the government (e.g. income tax)

questions.question_text: Explain two likely effects of the higher income tax personal allowance on Halcyon Motors.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Higher disposable income for buyers [k], because households keep an extra $1,500 a year after the allowance rises from $12,000 to $13,500 [app]. Effect 2: Increased demand for cars [k], so the director expects sales to rise above last year's 160 cars and $3,200,000 revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: higher disposable income for consumers
increased demand for cars / big-ticket goods
application_max_2: allowance rises from $12,000 to $13,500 / extra $1,500 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the higher allowance could affect Halcyon's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: More money available [k], so households can afford a larger deposit or higher monthly payments on a family car [app], making new cars more accessible [an]. Way 2: The ability to trade up [k], as the extra $1,500 a year lets customers move from used to new models or choose better-specified cars [app], increasing the average transaction value for the dealership [an].

knowledge_max_2: more money available / larger deposits or payments
customers trade up / choose better-specified cars
application_max_2: family car / monthly payments on a car
analysis_max_2: new cars become more accessible
average transaction value rises

questions.question_text: Do you think Halcyon Motors should order more new-car stock rather than expand its used-car operation? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Ordering more new-car stock matches the expected demand surge [k], positioning Halcyon to sell to families keeping an extra $1,500 a year after the allowance rise [app], which could lift unit sales above last year's 160 cars and $3,200,000 revenue [an]. However, used cars offer lower profit per unit but lower risk [k], and expanding part-exchange builds stock cheaply while new cars tie up capital in unsold inventory [app], which could hurt cash flow if demand disappoints [an]. On one hand, new-car stock captures the tax-cut upside [eval]; on the other hand, expanding used cars is flexible if the recovery is slow [eval]. Overall, Halcyon should order more new-car stock cautiously, because consumer confidence and real disposable incomes are rising, but it should size orders to a few months' anticipated sales rather than over-committing.

knowledge_max_2: new-car stock matches expected demand
used cars are lower profit but lower risk
application_max_2: extra $1,500 a year after the allowance rise
analysis_max_2: new stock lifts revenue if demand recovers
unsold new cars tie up capital and hurt cash flow
evaluation_max_2: weighs new-car upside against used-car flexibility
justified recommendation with cautious order sizing

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
The Gilded Fork is a private limited company operating 4 casual restaurants in Country X. It employs 38 kitchen and floor staff across the sites and reported sales of $2,070,000 last year, with an average meal bill of $45 and sales of 46,000 meals served at or near full capacity.

The Country X government has announced a temporary cut in VAT on hospitality from 13.5% to 9% for 12 months, aimed at reviving the restaurant sector after a difficult downturn in trading across the whole country. Management must decide whether to pass the cut on to customers through lower menu prices or to keep prices completely unchanged and retain the extra margin to rebuild cash reserves after a difficult trading year.

questions.question_text: Define 'indirect tax'.
questions.model_answer: A tax charged on spending on goods and services, collected by the seller on behalf of the government, such as VAT [2].

knowledge_max_2: tax on spending / goods and services
collected by seller on behalf of government (e.g. VAT)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the VAT cut on The Gilded Fork.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Either a higher margin or lower prices [k], because the cut from 13.5% to 9% lets the restaurants keep more of the $45 average meal bill or pass savings to diners [app]. Effect 2: A potential boost to demand [k], as cheaper meals may lift sales above the 46,000 meals served last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: choice between higher margin or lower prices
potential boost to demand
application_max_2: cut from 13.5% to 9% / $45 average meal bill

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the VAT cut could affect the restaurant's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Lower prices if the cut is passed on [k], so customers pay less for their average $45 meal [app], stretching household budgets further during the difficult downturn [an]. Way 2: Better value for money [k], encouraging customers to dine out more than the 46,000 meals served last year [app], supporting the hospitality sector's recovery [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower prices if cut passed on
better value for money / more dining out
analysis_max_2: stretches household budgets
supports the hospitality sector's recovery

questions.question_text: Do you think The Gilded Fork should pass the VAT cut on to customers rather than keep menu prices unchanged? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Passing the cut on lowers dining-out costs [k], stretching the $45 average meal bill further for customers after a difficult downturn [app], which should increase meal covers above the 46,000 served last year and restore lost business [an]. However, keeping prices unchanged rebuilds cash [k], converting the 4.5 percentage point VAT cut straight into margin on $2,070,000 of sales [app], which strengthens the business after a difficult year [an]. On one hand, passing on the cut wins share and goodwill quickly [eval]; on the other hand, retaining margin protects jobs and supplier payments in a fragile sector [eval]. Overall, The Gilded Fork should pass on most of the cut through slightly lower prices, because the cut is temporary for 12 months and stimulating demand now is the fastest way to restore $2,070,000 or higher sales.

knowledge_max_2: passing on the cut lowers prices / stretches budgets
keeping prices rebuilds cash / protects jobs
application_max_2: 4.5 percentage point cut on $2,070,000 of sales
analysis_max_2: lower prices restore lost business quickly
retained margin strengthens cash and supplier payments
evaluation_max_2: weighs goodwill and share gains against cash rebuilding
justified recommendation referencing the 12-month window
